source: Malberg et al. (2025) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: 30 cognitive biases tested on 20 LLMs with 30,000 generated tests. Fundamental attribution error (FAE) was one of the weakest biases found.
numbers: FAE mean bias score 0.10 across 20 models (per-model range about -0.02 to 0.23). Compare information bias 0.54, in-group bias 0.41, self-serving bias 0.21, stereotyping 0.09.
limits: Score is the paper's own normalised bias score, not a human effect size. Some models score near 0 or slightly negative.
agent_relevance: Do not expect a strong FAE in a base model; test the chosen model.

source: Malberg et al. (2025) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: FAE test design: actor-observer perspective. A controversial action is described. The model is told it is the actor (control) or the observer (treatment). It picks the best explanation from matched dispositional and situational options on a 7-point Likert scale.
numbers: Bias score is the gap between role conditions in preference for dispositional explanations. Method follows Flick and Schweitzer 2021, Hooper et al. 2015, Riggio and Garcia 2009.
limits: Role is only a prompt label, no real stakes. Single paradigm; does not test the Jones-Harris attitude attribution design.
agent_relevance: A cheap template: swap 'you did X' for 'they did X' and compare the causes given. Usable as a check inside a self-critique step.

source: Malberg et al. (2025) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: In the same benchmark, self-serving bias (credit success to self, blame failure on others) is stronger than FAE for some models.
numbers: Self-serving bias mean 0.21; per-model values from -0.04 to 0.79 (one model 0.79, another 0.59, many near 0.0 to 0.1).
limits: Large spread across models; the mean hides near-zero models.
agent_relevance: Attribution bias depends on the model; measure it before relying on it.

source: Raj et al. (2026) Talent or Luck? Evaluating Attribution Bias in Large Language Models
finding: Attribution-theory benchmark of 140k prompts, 10 scenarios, 4 identity dimensions (gender, race, religion, nationality). Three settings: Single-Actor, Actor-Actor, Actor-Observer. Models choose among effort, ability (internal) and task difficulty, luck (external).
numbers: Models: Aya-Expanse-8B, Qwen-32B, Llama-3.3-70B (plus Llama 3.2-1B and 3.1-8B for size trends). 140k prompts total.
limits: Log-probability forced choice; only open models; no human baseline on the same prompts.
agent_relevance: Directly measures internal versus external causal attribution in LLMs and shows identity cues shift it.

source: Raj et al. (2026) Talent or Luck? Evaluating Attribution Bias in Large Language Models
finding: Models differ in default style. Aya-Expanse-8B leans to external causes. Qwen-32B and Llama-3.3-70B lean to internal causes.
numbers: Radar plots of log-probabilities across effort, ability, difficulty, luck (Figure 3); no single numeric table in the text.
limits: Style differs by model, so one 'LLM attribution style' claim is not safe.
agent_relevance: Test the base model's default attribution lean before using it to explain failures.

source: Raj et al. (2026) Talent or Luck? Evaluating Attribution Bias in Large Language Models
finding: With an actor present, Qwen externalises success (luck, ease) while all models internalise failure (low effort or ability).
numbers: Reported as effect-size shifts d by identity; all three models show internalised failure.
limits: Effect sizes per identity pair are small and mixed in direction.
agent_relevance: When an agent explains another agent's failure it may blame the agent (disposition) over the situation, a risk in multi-agent debugging.

source: Raj et al. (2026) Talent or Luck? Evaluating Attribution Bias in Large Language Models
finding: Actor-Actor pairings: when two identities co-occur, models give less internal credit for success and more internal blame for failure. African, Greek, German actors tend to have success externalised and failure internalised.
numbers: Directional effect sizes per nationality pair; in Aya, female actors paired with Japanese or Korean identities more often had success internalised.
limits: Template-based; not tested against human data.
agent_relevance: Identity labels change attribution; a neutral scaffold should strip identity cues before causal explanation.

source: Raj et al. (2026) Talent or Luck? Evaluating Attribution Bias in Large Language Models
finding: Actor-Observer: adding an observer identity amplifies attribution shifts mostly for external causes (difficulty, luck). Larger models are more sensitive to identity than the 8B model.
numbers: Qwen-32B and Llama-3.3-70B show clearly negative shifts when identity is added; Aya-8B stays stable. Effort and ability change little.
limits: Strongest in healthcare and workplace scenarios.
agent_relevance: Bigger models may be more identity sensitive, which is not the same as less biased.

source: Raj et al. (2026) Talent or Luck? Evaluating Attribution Bias in Large Language Models
finding: Pipeline check: matching percentages stay high across nationality, race and religion.
numbers: Llama-3.3-70B nationality (300) 85.3%, religion 89.2%; Aya-8B nationality (600) 79.7%; Qwen-32B nationality 79.5%; third column 62.0% to 84.6%.
limits: Robustness check, not a human comparison.
agent_relevance: Shows the harness is stable, so differences are not noise.

source: Trott and Walker (2023) GPT-4 correspondence bias test (blog post by Sean Trott)
finding: Jones-Harris style test on GPT-4. Essays from ProCon.org (gun control, abortion, fur) were presented as written by someone assigned the position under 4 levels of situational pressure. GPT-4 rated the writer's attitude 1 to 10.
numbers: Pressure levels include 1% extra credit (weak), threat of expulsion, gun at the head (strong). No exact means or N in the post. Manipulation check passed.
limits: Blog post only, no values, not peer reviewed. Paper cites Walker and Vul, Reconsidering the bias in the correspondence bias.
agent_relevance: Under weak pressure GPT-4 inferred attitudes from the essay stance (classic correspondence bias). Under strong pressure it stayed near neutral, like rational discounting.

source: Trott and Walker (2023) GPT-4 correspondence bias test (blog post by Sean Trott)
finding: The authors frame the bias as context-sensitive inference, not a fixed error.
numbers: Qualitative; Figure 1 shows graded fall of inferred attitude as pressure rises.
limits: One model, few essay topics.
agent_relevance: Supports supplying explicit situational-pressure facts so the model can discount them.

source: Jin, Zhang, Shu, Cui (2023) The Cultural Psychology of Large Language Models: Is ChatGPT a Holistic or Analytic Thinker?
finding: Analysis-Holism Scale (24 items, includes a causality subscale: interactionism versus dispositionism). GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 both scored more holistic than the human norm.
numbers: AHS: GPT-3.5 M=5.35 (SD 0.11, 10 runs), GPT-4 M=5.01 (SD 0.10) versus human norm 4.87 (SD 0.49, N=702); both p<.001.
limits: 10 runs per condition at temperature 1; self-report scale answered by a model, not behaviour. Causality subscale not reported alone.
agent_relevance: Cannot tell if the model is situationalist on attribution specifically.

source: Jin, Zhang, Shu, Cui (2023) The Cultural Psychology of Large Language Models: Is ChatGPT a Holistic or Analytic Thinker?
finding: Triadic Categorization Task (implicit measure): both models gave many relation-based (holistic) groupings.
numbers: TCT: GPT-3.5 0.87 (SD 0.06), GPT-4 0.85 (SD 0.05); above most Chinese provinces' mean in cited human data. No formal norm.
limits: Informal comparison; 10 runs.
agent_relevance: Implicit task agrees with the scale: base model closer to East Asian holistic style on cognitive process.

source: Jin, Zhang, Shu, Cui (2023) The Cultural Psychology of Large Language Models: Is ChatGPT a Holistic or Analytic Thinker?
finding: Value measures do not follow. Dialectical Self Scale and Self-construal Scale give mixed results.
numbers: DSS: GPT-3.5 4.59 vs norm 4.00 (N=158) p<.001; GPT-4 3.97, p=.344. SCS-Independent: GPT-3.5 6.98, GPT-4 5.32 vs 4.73 (N=382), both p<.001. SCS-Interdependent: GPT-3.5 5.85 (p<.001), GPT-4 4.95 vs 4.81 (p=.07).
limits: Authors suggest training data and RLHF as causes; not tested. GPT-3.5 near ceiling.
agent_relevance: Cognitive style and values are separable in the model.

source: Jin, Zhang, Shu, Cui (2023) The Cultural Psychology of Large Language Models: Is ChatGPT a Holistic or Analytic Thinker?
finding: Results are robust to temperature and prompt wording changes.
numbers: Figure 1: temperature sweep and varied prompt wording kept all findings; SD is zero at temperature 0.
limits: Only GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; no Chinese-trained models.
agent_relevance: Cheap robustness check to copy before trusting any attribution result.

source: Tao, Viberg, Baker, Kizilcec (2024) Cultural Bias and Cultural Alignment of Large Language Models
finding: Five OpenAI models compared with Integrated Values Survey data. All resemble English-speaking and Protestant European countries in values.
numbers: Closest countries without prompting include Finland (d=0.20), Andorra (d=0.21), Netherlands (d=0.45) on the Inglehart-Welzel map.
limits: Measures values, not attribution style.
agent_relevance: Default cultural prior of the base model is Western; other styles need prompting.

source: Tao, Viberg, Baker, Kizilcec (2024) Cultural Bias and Cultural Alignment of Large Language Models
finding: Cultural prompting (answer as a person from country X) moves answers closer to the target country for recent models.
numbers: Improves alignment for 71-81% of countries for GPT-4, 4-turbo, 4o. Mean cultural distance GPT-4o 2.42 to 1.57, GPT-4-turbo 2.71 to 1.77, GPT-4 2.69 to 1.65 (all P<.001). Less effective for GPT-3 and 3.5-turbo.
limits: About 20-30% of countries do not improve; distance stays well above zero.
agent_relevance: A one-line persona prompt is a cheap but partial control for culture-dependent explanation.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs
finding: An actor-observer asymmetry in models: the same error is corrected when it appears as a user message (external) but not as the model's own prior output (internal).
numbers: 14 open-source non-reasoning models: average blind spot 64.5%; Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Claude Sonnet 4 41.4%; 62.8% average on non-math BIG-Bench Mistake tasks.
limits: Non-reasoning models; injected errors; framed as activation failure not knowledge gap.
agent_relevance: Agents should re-read their own output as if written by someone else.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs
finding: Appending the word Wait after the model's own erroneous output reduces the blind spot, with no training.
numbers: Blind spot reduced 89.3% on average; mean accuracy up 156%. But and However work less well. Fine-tuning on 5,306 correction traces cuts it 76.0%.
limits: Measured on injected errors; Wait works through a nearly independent pathway from the role direction.
agent_relevance: Cheapest known scaffold for turning self-view into observer-view; candidate operator.

source: Kim, Yu, Yi (2026) The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows
finding: Conceptual paper. Users credit their own competence for LLM-produced output: an attribution error on the human side.
numbers: No experiments, no numbers; typology across computational, linguistic, analytical, creative domains.
limits: Theory only; calls for empirical validation.
agent_relevance: Agent logs should mark which steps the model did and which the user supplied.

source: Ma et al. (2026) DoVer: Intervention-Driven Auto Debugging for LLM Multi-Agent Systems
finding: Log-only blame to one agent and one step is often ill-posed: several different interventions can each repair the same failure. DoVer tests hypotheses by intervening.
numbers: Flips 18% and 28% of failed trials on AssistantBench and GAIA-derived sets; 49% (198 trials) on GSMPlus with AG2; validates or refutes 30-60% of hypotheses; up to 16% milestone progress.
limits: Magnetic-One and AG2 only; needs intervention budget.
agent_relevance: Counterfactual (interventionist) causal attribution instead of guessing from logs.

source: Ma et al. (2026) DoVer: Intervention-Driven Auto Debugging for LLM Multi-Agent Systems
finding: Ground-truth uncertainty affects step attribution scores.
numbers: 29 cases: the 14 uncertain give GPT-4o 24% and GPT-5 7% step accuracy; the 15 certain give GPT-4o 44% and GPT-5 53%.
limits: Small N.
agent_relevance: Single-cause blame is not well defined; allow multiple causes.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? (Who&When)
finding: Benchmark for automated failure attribution: logs from 127 multi-agent systems, 184 annotation tasks labelled by agent and decisive error step. Models do poorly.
numbers: Best method 53.5% agent-level and 14.2% step-level accuracy; best 8.77% step accuracy on hand-crafted systems; o1 and R1 also not practical.
limits: Annotation uncertainty rates 16.7% to 26.3% by annotator; some methods below random.
agent_relevance: LLM blame at step level is weak; do not trust single-pass blame in a self-repair loop.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? (Who&When)
finding: Three prompting methods trade off: all-at-once, step-by-step, binary search. All-at-once is best on who; step-by-step best on when.
numbers: All-at-once agent-level accuracy exceeds step-by-step by about 19 to 21 points in the ground-truth judging setting; ranking reverses at step level.
limits: Depends on context length.
agent_relevance: Scaffold choice changes the answer: wide pass for the agent, stepwise pass for the step.

source: Rosenblum, Lazebnik, Ben-Zion (2026) Being judged through the record: A Rosenhan-inspired test of psychiatric label sensitivity in LLMs
finding: A stable-trait label overrides identical current evidence. Five LLMs, 20,000 responses.
numbers: When evidence supported discharge, a prior schizophrenia label raised continued-hospitalisation advice from 4.7% (237/5,000) to 22.3% (1,113/5,000); risk difference 17.5 points (95% CI 16.2-18.8); range 10.4-34.4 across models. Concordance fell 95.3% to 77.7% while confidence rose, d=0.35-1.09.
limits: Vignette study, not real patients. When evidence supported hospitalisation the label moved 92.6% to 97.0%.
agent_relevance: Guard against stale dispositional labels in agent memory.

source: Huynh, Lentz, van Miltenburg (2022) Implicit causality in GPT-2: a case study
finding: GPT-2 reproduces human implicit-causality bias (verbs that point the cause to subject or object) in pronoun surprisal, but continuation quality is weak.
numbers: Verb frequency effect b=-0.049 (SE 0.012, p<.01); fixed effects R2=.142, with random effects R2=.230; only 32% of continuations had mean rating >=4 on a 5-point scale.
limits: GPT-2 only; chance level for female subjects with subject-biased verbs; authors say superficial heuristics.
agent_relevance: Language statistics carry a causal-attribution bias that models pick up with shallow understanding.

source: Nisbett, Peng, Choi, Norenzayan (2001) Culture and systems of thought: holistic versus analytic cognition
finding: Human baseline source for the situational vs dispositional claim. Not opened this session.
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Reference for human baseline.

source: Search gap note: no LLM replication of Morris and Peng 1994 or Choi et al. 1999 found
finding: arXiv searches for cross-cultural causal attribution in LLMs returned only Jin et al. (holism scales) and Tao et al. (values). No direct replication of cultural attribution findings was found.
numbers: 0 direct replications found; arXiv API, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were rate limited; 1 of 6 web searches ran.
limits: Absence not proven.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on LLM-specific cultural attribution results.

source: Cao (n.d.) LLM self-serving bias and FAE (secondary mention via search summary)
finding: Search summary says LLMs show self-serving bias consistently but FAE not uniformly across models. Original paper not found or opened.
numbers: None.
limits: Secondary and unverified.
agent_relevance: Consistent with Malberg et al.
